projects.title: Tesla | Mechanical Design Engineer Intern
projects.content: Led design and development of seven thermal coolant components for CyberCab and other vehicles.Managed RFQs, DFM reviews, and approved $160,000 in tooling for $1M+ annual components.Optimized thermal designs using first-principles engineering, saving $100,000+ annually.Directed investigations on automation, NVH, and insulation, performing eight tests and analyzing data.  I had the incredible opportunity to work as a Mechanical Design Engineer in the Bay Area, USA, as part of the Thermal Team, which is known for owning one of the best-engineered vehicle thermal systems in the world.As a key member of the thermal team, I was responsible for seven thermal coolant hose bundles spanning two future vehicles (CyberCab and Cybertruck RWD). I led various investigations, from material selection to automation design. My role involved the full iterative process of design, prototyping, and testing, gaining hands-on experience in designing for manufacturing (DFM) and automation.One of my significant contributions was leading the RFQ (Request for Quote) process for one of the future vehicles. This included coordinating ongoing meetings with multiple suppliers to ensure the design was ready for mass production. My efforts culminated in giving the go-ahead for over $160k in tools, which helped the company save over $100k annually, all while the components were projected to cost over $1 million a year.What stood out most during my time at Tesla was the company's unique flat organizational structure. Despite the global challenges faced by large tech companies, Tesla operates with a lean, trusting approach that places significant ownership in its employees. This allowed me to accomplish and grow in ways I never expected, and I'm incredibly grateful for the opportunity.Applying the knowledge I gained at Monash University, including Solid Mechanics, Dynamics, Thermal, Materials, and Tolerancing, was instrumental in my day-to-day work. I also expanded my knowledge with new topics like NVH (Noise, Vibration, and Harshness) and durability, which were critical in ensuring the success of my projects. Tesla Website    LinkedIn Post

projects.title: Big Dipper Challenge (ELO2, NASA) | Lead Mechanical Design Engineer
projects.content: Led a two-person team to 1st place ($2,100), designing an innovative excavation system by conducting in-depth research, refining project requirements, and creating a lightweight, space-efficient solution that reduced weight to 8.75% and volume to 11% of constraints, while delivering comprehensive engineering reports and a presentation video.  NASA's Artemis program aims to return astronauts to the moon after over 50 years. In collaboration with a global alliance, Australia has been invited to design a lunar rover for collecting regolith samples. ELO2, a leading consortium competing for the opportunity to develop the first Australian lunar rover, initiated the Big Dipper Lunar Regolith Acquisition Challenge to innovate (lunar) excavation methods which have not really changed over the past 200+ years. This challenge aimed to design an innovative Regolith Sample Acquisition Device that could be attached to an Australian-designed rover for collecting and depositing lunar regolith at an In-situ Resource Utilisation (ISRU) facility operated by NASA on the moon.       I formed and led a two-person team to take part in this exciting challenge. After meticulously breaking down the problem, considering all design aspects, conducting extensive research, and brainstorming countless solutions that met the project requirements, we finalized on one solution that we went on to further develop and refine, called - ROMEO. ROMEO leverages electromagnetics for lunar sample collection in low-gravity environments. Ultimately, we enjoyed the challenge and were humbled to have emerged as the 1st place winners in the national competition, marking a significant achievement in pushing the boundaries of lunar exploration.               Our Winning Solution:     ROMEO, which stands for Regolith Oxygen Magnetic Extraction Operative, is a groundbreaking lunar excavation solution set to revolutionize lunar regolith collection for oxygen extraction. By leveraging the magnetic properties of lunar regolith, which contains oxygen-rich, ferrous materials, ROMEO's magnetic extraction provides an additional filter for the regolith, ensuring unparalleled efficiency in later oxygen extraction.     In essence, ROMEO is a brushless motor-driven circular drum with six strategically positioned ferromagnetic solenoids, ensuring precise regolith attraction and collection. Linear rails, combined with a LIDAR sensor, provide consistent lowering of the system and incorporate feedback loops to maintain a reliable 1-5mm distance above the lunar surface during excavation. After just 5 revolutions, ROMEO's hopper will conservatively hold 219g of regolith, and a linear actuator trap door system can then be employed to deposit the regolith in a controlled manner.     This excavation mechanism seamlessly integrates with the Trailblazer rover, weighing a mere 1.75kg and occupying only approximately 11% of the available volume. Overall, ROMEO's unique design ensures lunar stability, marking a paradigm shift in regolith acquisition technology.     As ROMEO progresses through the active design phase at Technology Readiness Level 3, it emerges as a creative and efficient solution, blending electromagnetism and cutting-edge engineering to address the lunar regolith collection challenge with unparalleled ingenuity. projects.title: 3D Printer Hotend Challenge | Lead Mechanical Engineer
projects.content: Increased Modix 3D printer flowrate by 127%, reaching 166mm³/s.Benchmarked E3D V6 hotend using ANSYS simulations, hand calculations, and physical tests.Designed a new hotend to enhance thermal efficiency and flowrate. The goal of this project was to increase the flowrate performance of the Modix 3D Printer by at least 20%. As the Lead Engineering and Thermal Mechanical Engineer, I managed a team of five engineers, overseeing project scope, timelines, and the collaborative design process.My team's first task was to evaluate the performance of the current hotend, the E3D V6, using thermal benchmarking methods such as hand calculations, ANSYS simulations, and physical testing with a heat gun. Based on these findings, we moved forward with designing our own hotend, focusing on improving thermal efficiency and overall flowrate.I contributed to solution generation and the final design, ensuring the hotend met the performance requirements. I also managed material selection and sourcing, and performed extensive thermal analysis on the final design.The project culminated in machining the final hotend on an Okuma 5-axis CNC, and the results were impressive: physical testing showed a 127% increase in flowrate, with the new hotend achieving a flowrate of 166mm³/s, well above the target. CFD simulations of the fan ducts also looked promising, further validating the design.This experience allowed me to develop my leadership skills, perform in-depth thermal and fluid analysis, and deliver a high-performance design that exceeded expectations. projects.title: Engineering Innovation Challenge 2023 | Lead Mechatronics Engineer
projects.content: Led a three-person team to 1st place ($10,000) in a global competition, surpassing 137 teams.Developed a 1:32 scale flood-proof road prototype through research, procurement, manufacturing, and testing.Delivered detailed reports and a compelling presentation on methodology and outcomes. In 2023, I assembled and led a dedicated team of three engineers to partake in the prestigious global competition, known as the Engineering Innovation Challenge (EIC), hosted in Singapore. The focal point of the 2023 challenge revolved around 'Engineering for Resilient City Living.' Over an intensive five-month period, my team and I directed unwavering attention to tackle the complex issue of flash flooding, culminating in the innovative concept of flood-proof roads.       With the submission of a comprehensive concept report, our remarkable journey did not end there, as we advanced to the highly competitive final round. For the final round, we secured crucial prototype funding, propelling us toward the realisation of a 1:32 small-scale proof of concept. Overall, our dedication to the challenge resulted in the creation of a prototype, a well-written final report, and an engaging 10-minute presentation to esteemed judges based in Singapore.       What makes our achievement truly exceptional is the fact that this marked our debut in the competition, and we triumphed over 137 teams from around the world, securing the coveted 1st place in the highest category. Our victory etched a significant milestone in EIC's 14-year history as the first international team to claim the top spot. The distinguished announcement came during the grand award ceremony on August 26th, with the Deputy Prime Minister of Singapore, Mr. Heng Swee Keat, bestowing us with this historic honor. projects.title: Monash Nova Rover | Mechanical Engineer
projects.content: Led design, prototyping, and assembly of payload housings, science platform, and excavation mechanism, achieving efficient life detection and excavation of 54kg regolith in 20 minutes, securing 1st place in Australia and 2nd globally in 2022 and 2023.Designed a four-wheel suspension linkage, reducing rover weight by 33% and costs by 60%, with pivot steering, contributing to global competition success. I joined Monash Nova Rover in 2021, driven by my passion for space technology and a deep eagerness to learn. My contributions in the Science sub-team were pivotal, where I played a major role in the design, prototyping, and assembly of two science payload housings, including platform, PCB mount, tube gantry, battery mount, snoop, and more. I quickly became proficient in SolidWorks, Cura, and FDM 3D printing, while gaining hands-on experience with various fabrication tools.       Within days of joining, I was fully immersed in the team's projects, and our efforts paid off at the Australian Rover Challenge (ARC), where Nova Rover secured 1st place in Australia. Shortly after, we competed in the University Rover Challenge (URC) in Utah, focused on Mars exploration. Despite my short tenure on the team, I was honored to be one of the 23 members representing Nova Rover in Utah. We placed 2nd globally in 2022, missing 1st by only 8.42 points.                          In the following design cycle, I expanded my involvement beyond Science, contributing to the Chassis sub-team. The Chassis team transitioned from a six-wheel drive to a four-wheel drive system with pivot steering, while the Science team developed new excavation and Martian life detection mechanisms. I collaborated on designing the 4-wheel suspension system and the novel scraper excavation mechanism, applying my prior NASA prototyping experience.       Our efforts led to back-to-back successes, with Nova Rover securing 1st place in Australia and 2nd place in the world in 2023. Looking back, I am immensely proud of this journey and excited to see Nova Rover continue pushing boundaries in robotics and planetary exploration. projects.title: Hoisting Platform | Mechanical Design Engineer
projects.content: Led a team of four engineers to design a system for transporting an engineer up a wind turbine, focusing on the hoisting platform, motor, materials, and load calculations.Conducted Finite Element Analysis (FEA) and designed shafts, pinions, and racks with a safety factor of 3.Gained experience in mechanical design, load analysis, FEA, and project management, culminating in a 93-page report documenting the system's proof of concept.  I led a team of four engineers to design a system that would transport an engineer from the base of a wind turbine to the top. In the preliminary design phase, I was responsible for designing the hoisting platform that would safely lift the engineer, contributing to motor selection, material selection, and general load calculations. We compiled our considerations into a comprehensive report.       During the final design stage, my team and I conducted Finite Element Analysis (FEA) and designed the necessary shafts, pinions, and racks capable of supporting the engineer and the platform with a safety factor of at least 3. This culminated in the completion of a 93-page report detailing the system's proof of concept.       This project provided me with invaluable hands-on experience in mechanical design, load analysis, and the practical application of FEA, while also refining my skills in team collaboration and project management. projects.title: TOM | Mechanical Engineer
projects.content: Contributed to a project at TOM Melbourne Makeathon to design a custom head support for a woman with Scoliosis and Parkinson's.Worked with a team to improve her posture and reduce health risks through a tailored wheelchair solution.Applied engineering skills to create a real-world impact and gained valuable insights into inclusive design. TOM (Tikkun Olam Makers) is a global movement that designs and creates affordable solutions for neglected challenges faced by people with disabilities, the elderly, and those living in poverty. In 2022, I had the privilege of joining the TOM Melbourne Makeathon, where my team and I worked on a project aimed at improving the life of Joan, a woman living with Scoliosis and Parkinson's.       Joan's condition causes her to lean excessively to the right without realizing it, which poses a major health risk. Our goal was to enhance her wheelchair to help correct her posture and reduce this risk.       With only 48 hours to design, prototype, and build a final solution, we worked tirelessly to meet the deadline. My role involved designing and building a head support that attaches to Joan's existing wheelchair headrest. I used a jigsaw to cut the support from aluminum, bent it for ergonomic comfort, sanded the edges to remove sharp points, and added padding for comfort. To finish, I sewed a cover for the headrest to make it aesthetically pleasing.       By the end of the weekend, our team successfully created four different systems that greatly improved Joan's posture. We also met again a few weeks later to make adjustments and ensure Joan could get the best use out of our design.       This experience was incredibly rewarding, as it allowed me to apply my engineering skills to make a real difference in someone's life. It also deepened my understanding of inclusive design, a lesson that will stay with me throughout my career. TOM Global    TOM Melbourne    LinkedIn Post on TOM

projects.title: Teleoperation of Kuka Robotic Arm | Software Engineer
projects.content: I led a team of three in developing an integrated virtual reality system designed to enhance user control and precision in teleoperating robotic arms. This system, implemented in the Monash Smart Manufacturing Hub's Digital Twin Lab, enables intuitive real-time manipulation of a KUKA robotic arm using VR hand-tracking and an advanced two-finger haptic feedback glove. Working every day for three months over the summer, we achieved significant milestones. Haptic Glove I designed and tested seven iterations of the glove, sourced components, created the electrical schematic, soldered and crimped connections, and wrote Python scripts on a Raspberry Pi Model 4B to enable two-way communication with the robotic arm gripper. Additionally, I designed the housing for the Raspberry Pi. The haptic glove now functions seamlessly upon power-up.   Robotic Arm I wrote the KUKA Sunrise Java code that allows the robotic arm and end effector to receive values from the server, enabling real-time control. This required an in-depth understanding of OPC UA to create new variables, as well as extensive research into KUKA Sunrise and Robotiq Gripper 2F-140 documentation. Ultimately, I successfully integrated the gripper with both the KUKA robotic arm and the server. VR & Hand Tracking I developed the virtual lab environment that users interact with in VR. Additionally, I wrote C# scripts that track the user's hand, calculate movement differences, and transmit the data to the server for the robotic arm to mimic. I also wrote scripts for mapping gripper movement in Unity and learned how to integrate different robotic frames. Furthermore, I co-wrote the locomotion scripts that allow users to navigate the lab and authored the view-changer script, which lets users switch between different perspectives.     Camera Streams I sourced and implemented a Zed Camera, RealSense Camera, and LogiCamera, integrating them with a Xavier Jetson to enhance teleoperation by making control more immersive and intuitive.   Software Development My contributions extended to software development, where I wrote the code that connects the KUKA robotic arm to the server, implemented OPC UA for industrial communication, and developed the Unity-based control system for the gripper. Additionally, I engineered the hand-tracking system, calculated movement differences, and transmitted them to the server while integrating all camera streams for a seamless operator experience. Administration I formed and led the team, holding weekly meetings with our supervisor and bi-weekly meetings with the team. I also wrote all the necessary documentation to obtain ethics approval, including the Explanatory Statement, Consent Form, Interview Topics, and Survey Questions - ensuring we could conduct testing with participants. Additionally, I authored and secured approval for two detailed risk assessments, one for the project as a whole and another specifically for the full-body haptic suit, assuming the role of Risk Owner. I conducted extensive academic research in this field, developed a six-month project timeline (Gantt Chart), and contributed significantly to the project report.       Ultimately, this project was highly rewarding. By reducing cognitive strain and improving operational accuracy, we laid the groundwork for future advancements in haptic-enhanced teleoperation.
